title: Simulation of an inhomogeneous Fermi gas through the BCS-BEC crossover
abstract_summary: The authors perform variational quantum Monte Carlo simulations of the zero-temperature BCS–BEC crossover for a trapped, two-component Fermi gas (2N = 330) with a short-range attractive interaction. They propose compact one-parameter many-body trial wavefunctions built from two-body solutions, compute energies, densities and two-body correlations across the crossover, verify virial relations near unitarity, and estimate the universal parameter β ≈ −0.51.
methodology_description: The authors perform classical variational quantum Monte Carlo (VQMC) simulations to study the zero-temperature BCS–BEC crossover of a trapped two-component Fermi gas. They begin with an extensive analysis of the trapped two-body problem (relative and center-of-mass separation) for a short-range attractive potential V(r)=V0 exp(-2r/b) to obtain compact analytic approximations for two-body eigenfunctions and energies across scattering-length regimes. These two-body solutions are used as building blocks for many-body trial states. For weakly interacting (BCS-side) regimes they employ a Jastrow–Slater ansatz: a product of Slater determinants (one per spin) formed from harmonic-oscillator single-particle eigenfunctions and a pairwise Jastrow factor (two alternative Jastrow forms tested). For the crossover and BEC regimes they use an antisymmetrized product of paired two-body functions (Eagles–Leggett type), with pair functions taken from the trapped two-body solutions multiplied by a Gaussian center-of-mass factor exp(-λ|R|^2); λ is a variational parameter. Expectation values of the Hamiltonian are minimized with respect to the variational parameter(s) by Metropolis Monte Carlo sampling of |Ψ|^2. Energies are computed using local estimators and, where possible, kinetic contributions are handled by integration by parts to avoid explicit second derivatives. Simulations use closed-shell configurations (2N=330 total, N=165 per spin, MF=8 filled shells), potential ranges b/2 down to O(10^-3) (in units sqrt(ħ/mω)), and typical Monte Carlo runs with ≈10^3 thermalization steps and ≈10^4 sampling steps. Observables reported include energy per particle, trapping potential energy, optimized variational parameters, single-particle density profiles, two-particle correlation functions, and verification of virial relations across the crossover.
key_findings: [supported] Performed variational quantum Monte Carlo (VQMC) simulations of the zero-temperature BCS–BEC crossover for a trapped, inhomogeneous two-component Fermi gas with 2N = 330 particles (N = 165 per spin) using short-range attractive two-body interactions.

[supported] Constructed one-parameter variational many-body wave functions (Jastrow–Slater for weak attraction; Eagles–Leggett antisymmetrized pair product for crossover/strong coupling) informed by an analysis of the trapped two-body problem.

[supported] Developed efficient numerical techniques exploiting properties of antisymmetrized many-body functions (minors and inverse-matrix relations) enabling VQMC for unusually large particle numbers.

[supported] Found the virial relation between energy per particle and trapping energy to hold approximately over the interval −0.1 < 1/kF a < 3.4, comparing direct energy and trap-energy estimates and using virial expressions.
[supported] Determined an upper-bound estimate of the universal parameter at unitarity β = −0.51 ± 0.01 from the variational energies.

[supported] Observed that the Eagles–Leggett paired-wavefunction becomes energetically favorable relative to the Jastrow–Slater form for 1/kF a ≳ −0.45 (i.e., around that value pairing wavefunction yields lower energy), identifying a crossover onset in their variational comparison.

[supported] Reported a variational instability (collapse tendency) in the extreme BEC region when using purely attractive finite-range potentials; found local minima with λ_EL ≈ 1 for moderate positive 1/kF a but signaled finite-range artifacts for very large 1/kF a.
[supported] Found that the energy curve E(1/kF a), suitably normalized, is largely independent of the shell number MF (system size) and that its derivative exhibits a minimum at unitarity.

[supported] Computed one- and two-body correlation functions showing Pauli-blocking evolution with interaction strength and signatures of molecule formation on the BEC side; reported pair correlation lengths much larger than the interaction range.

[speculative] Suggested that adding a short-range repulsive component to the interaction could remove the variational instability in the deep BEC regime (proposal consistent with earlier theoretical suggestions).
[speculative] Noted that improved trial wave functions may reduce discrepancies with virial predictions in the BCS-to-crossover transition zone (recommendation for future work).
results_summary: The authors carried out large-scale variational quantum Monte Carlo simulations of a trapped two-component Fermi gas across the BCS–BEC crossover for 2N=330 particles. They designed compact one-parameter trial wave functions guided by an analytic study of the trapped two-body problem and implemented efficient evaluation algorithms for antisymmetrized pair-product states. Their simulations produce energies, radii and correlation functions across the crossover, verify approximate virial relations over −0.1 < 1/kF a < 3.4, identify the pairing-wavefunction as energetically preferable beyond 1/kF a ≈ −0.45, and yield an upper-bound estimate β = −0.51 ± 0.01 at unitarity. They also report a variational instability in the extreme BEC limit due to finite-range attractive interactions and observe expected signatures of Pauli blocking and molecule formation in two-body correlations.
performance_claims: System size: 2N = 330 (N = 165 per spin state); closed-shell MF = 8 (examples also shown up to MF = 9).
Estimated universal parameter at unitarity: β = −0.51 ± 0.01 (upper bound from variational energies).
Approximate virial relation validity range: −0.1 < 1/kF a < 3.4 (agreement between E/2N and trap-energy estimates).
Crossover onset where paired (Eagles–Leggett) ansatz outperforms Jastrow–Slater: 1/kF a ≈ −0.45.
At unitarity, fitted linear relation for closed shells: EU/2N ≃ (0.53 ± 0.01) (MF + 1.95 ± 0.06) ħω.
Potential ranges used in simulations (examples): b/2 = 0.00375 √(ħ/mω) before unitarity and b/2 = 0.0025 √(ħ/mω) for kF a ≥ 0 (shortest reliable ranges reported).
quantum_advantage_detail: This paper presents classical variational quantum Monte Carlo simulations of many-body fermions (no quantum computing hardware, algorithms, or claims of quantum advantage are involved); thus claims about quantum computational advantage are not applicable.
limitations: Variational instability in the extreme BEC region due to the use of purely attractive finite-range potentials: the variational energy can collapse for large λEL and deep BEC parameters; authors note this instability and that it could be avoided by adding a short-distance repulsive term but that implementation is difficult given chosen parameter regime.

Use of a finite-range interaction (V(r)) rather than an idealized contact interaction: finite-range effects are non-negligible for deep BEC parameters (large positive 1/kF a) and produce quantitative discrepancies (e.g. two-body ground-state energies and failure of contact virial relations in that region).

Limited achievable potential range (b/2): the reported b/2 values are the shortest ranges for which the authors obtained reliable numerical results, i.e. numerical stability/accuracy prevented exploring arbitrarily smaller b/2.

Larger numerical errors and sampling difficulty at unitarity (|a| → ∞): the delocalized character of the paired two-body wavefunction at unitarity makes Monte Carlo evaluation of expectation values more difficult and yields larger uncertainties.

Statistical sampling challenges for extended clouds (BCS/weak-coupling side): evaluation of mean radii and energies for extended atom clouds requires special care and produced discrepancies with virial predictions in some regions.

The many-body variational ansatz is relatively simple (one-parameter families): the Eagles–Leggett and Jastrow–Slater one-parameter wave functions, while compact, are not fully flexible and produce noticeable discrepancies (e.g. ~15% in trap energy vs. virial expectation) in the crossover region, indicating the need for improved trial wave functions.
[inferred] The work is restricted to zero temperature and balanced spin populations: finite-temperature effects and imbalanced mixtures are not treated.

[inferred] No direct calculation of certain many-body observables relevant to superfluidity (e.g. pairing gap, condensate fraction, excitation spectrum) — the study focuses on energies, densities and two-body correlations.
[inferred] The single-channel model and chosen interaction form may omit multichannel Feshbach-resonance physics that could be relevant near some experimental resonances.

[inferred] Monte Carlo run lengths (∼10^3 thermalization + ∼10^4 data steps reported) may be modest for the most challenging regimes (unitarity, extended clouds), potentially limiting statistical precision.
open_questions: How to construct improved many-body trial wave functions that better describe the crossover transition zone (reduce the ~15% discrepancy with virial predictions) while remaining computationally tractable for large N?

What is the best practical way to include a short-distance repulsive core (or other stabilization mechanism) in the interaction to avoid variational collapse in the deep BEC region, given the numerical constraints on b?

How do finite-range interaction effects quantitatively map onto the contact-interaction (zero-range) limit across the entire crossover, and what is the correct procedure to extrapolate finite-b results to the contact case?

What are the limits of validity of the virial relations observed here? In particular, why do the virial relations hold approximately for −0.1 < 1/kF a < 3.4 but break down outside that window (both on the BCS and deep BEC sides)?
How robust is the reported upper bound for the universal parameter β (β ≈ −0.51 ± 0.01) with respect to changes in N, improved wave functions, and other numerical methods?
How would inclusion of finite temperature change the energies, densities, correlations and the applicability of virial theorems (connecting to the finite-T virial results reported elsewhere)?

How significant are molecule–molecule interactions (e.g. amm ≈ 0.6 a) and composite-boson effects in the BEC side for trapped systems with finite-range potentials, and how should they be incorporated in a many-body variational description?
Can the Monte Carlo sampling and numerical methods be improved to reduce errors at unitarity and for extended clouds (e.g. more advanced importance sampling, larger runs, alternative estimators)?
future_work: Develop improved variational trial wave functions (beyond the one-parameter Eagles–Leggett and Jastrow–Slater forms) to better describe the crossover transition zone and to reduce discrepancies with virial relations.
Implement and study the effect of a short-distance repulsive interaction (or other regularization) to prevent variational collapse in the deep BEC region and to model molecule–molecule repulsion.
Perform calculations with smaller potential ranges and/or controlled extrapolations to approach the true contact-interaction limit more closely, assessing finite-range systematic effects.
Improve Monte Carlo sampling and numerical methods (longer runs, variance reduction, importance sampling) to reduce uncertainties especially at unitarity and for extended clouds.
Extend the study to finite temperature and/or imbalanced spin populations to test the applicability of finite-T virial theorems and explore experimentally relevant regimes.
Compute additional many-body observables (e.g. pairing gap, condensate fraction, excitation properties) to characterize superfluid behavior more completely and compare with other many-body methods.
